title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether AI-generated writing feedback using ChatGPT (GPT-4) can function effectively as an automated writing evaluation approach for English as a new language (ENL) learners, and whether students prefer it over human tutor feedback. The paper is motivated by growing interest in using generative AI ethically in writing instruction, especially given the spread of tools such as Grammarly and ChatGPT. Importantly for the retrieval topic, this is not a direct comparison between ChatGPT and legacy automated writing evaluation tools such as Criterion, MI Write, PEG, NC Write, or eRevise; instead, it compares ChatGPT-generated feedback with human tutor feedback and also examines student perceptions of AI versus human feedback.

The study reports two longitudinal studies conducted during a shortened Spring 2023 semester. Study 1 used a six-week repeated-measures quasi-experimental design with 48 university ENL students: the experimental group received GPT-4-generated feedback on weekly 300-word academic paragraphs, while the control group received feedback from a human tutor in weekly 30-minute one-on-one sessions. GPT-4 feedback was generated using a structured prompt asking for comments on topic sentence, idea development, academic language, transitions, use of sources/evidence, and grammar. Students revised and resubmitted their drafts. Writing performance was measured with pretest and posttest writing tasks scored by two experienced raters using an analytic rubric covering content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence; inter-rater reliability was reported as good to excellent.

Study 2 examined perceptions in a separate sample of 43 ENL students who received both GPT-4 and human tutor feedback on weekly assignments and completed a weekly survey over six weeks. Survey items addressed satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference, with open-ended explanations analyzed thematically. Results from Study 1 showed no statistically significant difference in writing gains between the AI-feedback and human-feedback groups, suggesting that GPT-4 feedback did not outperform human tutors but produced similar short-term learning outcomes. Study 2 found student preference was nearly evenly split: some preferred human tutors for interactivity, engagement, and follow-up questions, while others preferred AI for clarity, specificity, consistency, and convenience.

Overall, the paper concludes that GPT-4-generated feedback can be incorporated into ENL essay evaluation without reducing short-term learning outcomes relative to human tutor feedback, but the authors recommend a blended approach that combines the specificity of AI feedback with the interpersonal and dialogic benefits of human support. The evidence is closest to higher-education ENL writing support rather than the target domain of direct high-school comparative studies against established secondary-school writing tools.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study with a comparison group, pre/post measurement, longitudinal implementation, and reported inter-rater reliability, but it is not an RCT and is conducted in higher education rather than grades 9-12. Credibility is reasonably strong, though relevance to the user's target population is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The main comparative academic outcome showed no significant advantage for GPT-4 feedback over the human-tutor comparator, and student preference outcomes were essentially split rather than showing clear benefit. For the target comparative question, impact is therefore best characterized as no clear impact.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4 via ChatGPT generated automated written feedback on university ENL students' 300-word academic paragraphs, targeting topic sentence quality, idea development, academic language, transitions, use of sources/evidence, and grammar in support of revision.

ChatGPT/GPT-4 was used as an automated writing evaluation-style language feedback tool for ENL essay revision, functioning similarly to an AI writing assistant rather than broader text generation for submission.

finding.finding_summary: In Study 1, a six-week repeated-measures quasi-experiment with university ENL learners found no statistically significant difference in writing gains between students receiving GPT-4-generated feedback and those receiving human tutor feedback. The group-by-time interaction was non-significant (F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063), and posttest differences were also non-significant (t=-0.539, p=0.591, Cohen's d=-0.156); both groups improved from pretest to posttest on an analytic writing rubric.
finding.measure: Pre/post academic writing scores on a 40-point analytic rubric assessing content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence; weekly 300-word paragraph writing tasks
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.063 for interaction; Cohen's d=-0.156 for posttest group difference
finding.std_deviation: Pre: EG SD=1.301, CG SD=1.391; Post: EG SD=1.908, CG SD=2.066

finding.finding_summary: In Study 2, student preference between AI-generated and human tutor feedback was nearly evenly split across six weeks among a separate ENL sample. Mean ratings were high for both feedback sources on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference (generally above 4 on a 5-point scale), with only slight overall advantages for human tutors on Likert means but a slight numerical edge for AI on the forced-choice weekly preference item (grand mean Q9=1.53, where 1.5 indicates an even split).
finding.measure: Weekly 5-point Likert survey on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and feedback preference, plus forced-choice preference item and qualitative comments
finding.std_deviation: Q9 grand SD=0.50; item-level SDs generally about 0.83-1.38 across weeks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-generated feedback may reduce educator time burden and scale individualized feedback in larger classes, but this was not directly measured empirically. Because no workload, turnaround-time, or cost data were collected, operational benefits remain speculative rather than demonstrated.
finding.measure: Teacher time-saving/workload reduction discussed conceptually only
